readerTitle: The $40 speaker that can't ship without an $0.80 chip
caseNote: 가상 사례 (블루투스 스피커 제조사, 레스토랑 그룹) + 실제 관찰 (2020~2022년 반도체 부족 시기의 중복 주문). 모든 수치는 설명용입니다.
insight: 재고 전략은 회사 전체에 하나가 아니라 부품마다 정하는 것이고, 주문량은 실제 수요가 아니라 불안의 크기일 수 있다.
misconception: 린(lean) 회사라면 모든 부품을 적시 생산 방식으로 들여와야 하고, 주문이 늘면 그만큼 수요가 늘어난 것이다.

sources.text: 공급망 관리의 표준 개념 (적시 생산 vs 안전 재고, 채찍 효과)
2020~2022년 반도체 부족 시기의 중복 주문과 이후 재고 과잉에 대한 업계 보도 (일반적 서술로만 사용)
스피커 제조사와 레스토랑 그룹의 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 채찍 효과 예시: 소매업체 평소 주당 2,000대 → 6,000대 주문(3배), 매장 판매는 10% 증가에 그침. 가상 수치입니다.
2020~2022년 반도체 부족 때 일부 구매자가 실제 필요보다 많이 주문했고, 이후 일부 칩 품목에서 재고 과잉이 나타났다는 서술은 업계 보도에 근거한 일반적 관찰입니다. 특정 기업명이나 수치는 넣지 않았습니다. 게시 전 1차 보도로 다시 확인하세요.

cards.title: The $40 speaker that can't ship without an $0.80 chip
body: A small company makes Bluetooth speakers. Each one has about 30 parts. Most are easy to buy from several suppliers.
One isn't. A tiny wireless chip comes from a single chip maker. Its delivery time just jumped from 8 weeks to over 26. Without it, nothing ships.

image.label: A speaker taken apart, one small chip glowing
image.brief: 분해된 블루투스 스피커 부품들이 테이블 위에 펼쳐져 있고, 그중 손톱만 한 칩 하나만 밝게 빛남. 칩 옆에 "$0.80", 스피커 옆에 "$40" 라벨. 실제 브랜드 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: The holiday season is coming.
body: You build 10,000 speakers a month. You've always ordered parts monthly, just before you need them. Now the chip takes half a year to arrive.

options.text: Keep ordering monthly. Holding stock is waste
options.feedback: Just in time saves cash only when parts arrive on time. With a 26-week wait, one late delivery stops every sale.

options.text: Buy six months of the chip. Keep every other part lean
options.feedback: This is just in time vs just in case, decided part by part. You pay to buffer the one cheap, scarce part you can't ship without.

options.text: Buy six months of all 30 parts, to be safe
options.feedback: You'd never run short, but you'd tie up cash in parts you can reorder in days. Just in case pays off only where supply is truly at risk.

cards.title: Just in case, but only where it counts.
body: Six months of chips is 60,000 chips at $0.80. That's **$48,000** sitting on a shelf.
Compare it with one month of stopped production: 10,000 speakers at $40 is $400,000 in lost sales.
The rule isn't "lean" or "safe" for the whole company. Buffer parts that are cheap, hard to replace and slow to arrive. Run everything else **just in time**.

image.label: Parts sorted into two bins: buffer and just in time
image.brief: 부품을 두 상자로 나눈 그림. 왼쪽 큰 상자 "Buffer"에는 칩 하나만 많이, 오른쪽 "Just in time" 상자에는 나사, 케이스, 스피커 콘 등 여러 부품이 조금씩. 깔끔한 인포그래픽 스타일.

cards.softwareNote: Cloud capacity works the same way. Most servers can be rented on demand, but scarce resources like certain high-end chips may need to be reserved ahead, even if some sits idle.

cards.title: A big retailer suddenly triples its order.
body: Your largest retailer usually orders 2,000 speakers a week. This week it wants 6,000. Its own store sales are up only about 10%.
Its buyers have heard about chip shortages too. What do you do?

options.text: Triple production and order more chips to match
options.feedback: That's the bullwhip effect: you'd treat fear-driven orders as demand. When the panic fades, you're left with chips and speakers no one needs.

options.text: Look at store sales, raise output a little, and share your supply plans
options.feedback: You respond to real demand, not to orders swollen by worry. Telling buyers what you can deliver also calms the urge to over-order.
It avoids the overreaction but ignores the real 10% rise. A partner left short may also start ordering from your rivals.

cards.title: Orders measure worry as well as demand.
body: The **bullwhip effect** is how small changes in what shoppers buy grow into big swings in orders as you move up the chain.
Here, store sales rose 10%. The retailer ordered 3 times more. If you then ordered extra chips, the chip maker would see an even bigger jump.
During the 2020–2022 chip shortage, buyers widely reported ordering more than they needed to get in line. Later, some chips piled up as excess stock.

image.label: A whip growing wider from store to chip maker
image.brief: 왼쪽 매장에서 오른쪽 칩 공장까지 이어지는 채찍 모양 곡선. 매장 쪽은 작은 물결 "+10%", 소매업체 "×3", 공장 쪽은 아주 큰 물결. 단순한 선 그림 스타일.

cards.title: Buffers can go stale.
body: Electronics change fast. If you redesign the speaker next year with a newer chip, a shelf of old chips may become worthless.
So size a buffer to the risk window, not to forever. And reading real demand needs real data. Retailers share store sales only when they trust you won't use it against them.

cards.title: Now it's a restaurant group.
body: You run five restaurants. News says avocados will be scarce for a few weeks. Each manager doubles their order to be safe.
Guacamole is one of your best sellers. What do you do?

options.feedback: Five managers padding at once is the bullwhip effect in one company. Avocados spoil, so the extra may end up in the bin.

options.text: Order centrally from real usage, plus a small buffer for the top dish
options.feedback: You use real demand to tame the bullwhip and keep a just-in-case buffer only where a shortage would hurt most.

options.text: Take guacamole off the menu until prices drop
options.feedback: It removes the risk, but also a best seller. It makes sense only if the shortage is long or prices become extreme.

cards.title: Buffer the scarce part. Read the real demand.
body: You used two ideas. **Just in time vs just in case:** decide part by part, and buffer only what is scarce and critical. **The bullwhip effect:** check orders against what end customers actually buy.
**Try it today:** list the three inputs you could least afford to run out of. For each, write how long it takes to arrive and how many weeks of stock you hold.
